---
title: "Protocol to result"
---

A trial's result begins as a sentence in a protocol and ends as a number in a table. Between
them sit an analysis plan, a programming specification, several datasets and a succession of
people, each interpreting the last one's work.

Put together, the ambition of ICH M11, USDM and CDISC's Analysis and Derivation Concepts is a
path from that sentence to that number where **every step is declared rather than implied** —
and where the declaration, not a program, is the thing a reviewer reads.

This book is a record of trying it: two endpoints of a public simulated oncology trial, taken
the whole way, with what worked and what did not.

Whether the ambition is worth the trouble comes down to what a loosely declared step costs. One
example, which the last chapter takes apart: the chain described here computes a treatment
difference, placebo minus torivumab, of **{{fact:lab.engine.diff|4}}**; the same model, fitted
by a programmer from the same plan on the study's own derived variables, computes
**{{fact:lab.reference.diff|4}}**.

Neither is wrong. They differ over which record is *baseline*. The plan is precise: the last
value on or before the first dose, chosen by date. The chain declared it as the record at the
Baseline visit, chosen by visit — and a subject can have two records there, a screening draw and
a pre-dose draw on the first day of treatment. The programmer's datasets carry the plan's rule
in a flag; the engine took the first record it found. On {{fact:lab.baseline.differ}} of
{{fact:lab.baseline.subjects}} subjects the two rules land on different rows.

The plan had said which. The declaration lost it on the way — one step, in the simplest endpoint
a trial has.

## Who this is for

Anyone in pharma. No CDISC background is assumed: terms are explained where they first matter,
and linked to their source rather than collected into a glossary you would have to read first.

You do not need to install anything to read it. If you want to *drive* it, one command sets up
everything, and the setup chapter covers it.

## How it is organised

One chapter per stage, in the order the work happens — from reading the protocol against a
structured template, through the concept model, to executing an analysis in the browser and
comparing the result against the datasets a programmer built from the same plan.

Every **stage** chapter answers the same four questions:

- **What this is** — the concept, in plain terms
- **What you do** — the actions, in order
- **What you should see** — the expected outcome
- **What to look out for** — where this went wrong for us, and why

That last section is the reason this exists. The standards documents describe the destination;
almost nothing describes the potholes.

**This is a book about the concepts, not about the tool.** One reference application is used
throughout, because concepts you cannot see working are hard to believe and impossible to check
— but it is the instrument, not the subject. So each chapter states the work first and then how
this particular application happens to do it, under *in the application used here*.

The same distinction applies to the potholes. Some are properties of the model and will be true
of any tool; others are true of this one, at the commit pinned here, and may already have been
fixed. The second kind carry a note saying so. It is worth knowing which is which before you
carry a lesson from this book to a tool that is not this one.

## Two ways in

Where you join depends on where your protocol came from, and it changes which chapters apply.

| | Stage 0 | Stage 0b | From stage 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Protocol authored to ICH M11** | Confirm the elements your endpoint needs are present and populated | *Does not apply* — nothing to restructure | Identical |
| **Protocol predates M11, or follows a sponsor template** | Map it, element by element, and record what is absent | Move the misplaced content, then regenerate | Identical |

This book walks the second, because the study it uses predates M11 — and because that is the
more common position today. The two converge at stage 1, and everything after it is the same
work either way.

Two later chapters assume something else again. **Stage 6 needs analysis datasets** to run
against; **stage 7 needs a second, independently built implementation** to compare with, which
exists when a study is being re-examined and not when one is being specified for the first time.
Each of those chapters says what to do without it. Stages 0 to 5 need only a protocol and a set
of definitions, and produce a specification whether or not any data exists.

## Two things to know before you start

**The numbers here are read from the runs, not typed.** Every figure is resolved from the
results files at build time, so a figure in this book and the run that produced it cannot
disagree. When the underlying study was regenerated and every number moved, the book moved
with it.

**It does not end in agreement.** The divergence this chapter opened with is where the book
finishes, taken apart rather than smoothed over.
